en: How a Crossing Became a Provincial Capital
ja: 渡し場はいかに省都になったか

p.src: Step from the shops of Zhangye Road into Lanzhou Prefecture City God Temple and the space changes to a sequence of courtyards. Grey tiles, painted brackets, and red columns share the view with surrounding apartment blocks. That contrast says more than calling Lanzhou an “ancient city”: a later prefectural-city layer remains visible, but it does not prove that the Han city stood beneath this courtyard. The compound is also used by Lanzhou First Workers' Club. At the entrance, check whether an event is taking place and which courtyards are accessible instead of relying on opening hours copied from an old guide.

caption.zh: 灰瓦、彩绘斗拱和红柱留在密集的现代街区里；先看当天能进入哪一进院落，再沿张掖路读老城。
caption.ja: 灰色の瓦、彩色の組物、赤い柱が密集した現代市街に残る。当日入れる中庭を確かめてから、張掖路で旧市街を読む。
caption.en: Grey tiles, painted brackets, and red columns survive inside a dense modern district. Check which courtyards are accessible that day, then read the old city along Zhangye Road.

p.src: The map gives one walking sequence: west along Zhangye Road from the provincial-government area, past the City God Temple and Xiguan, then north to the south end of Zhongshan Bridge. The former east and west gates are approximate historical locators, not entrances that survive today. The four coloured panels do not show four cities stacked on one footprint; they mark four stages in where the city worked and how people crossed the river. No walking time or temporary closure is encoded, so adjust the route to conditions on the day.

caption.zh: 从省政府一带沿张掖路向西，经城隍庙和西关再转向桥边；旧城门只是约位，汉代金城县治也不画成确定城址。
caption.ja: 省政府周辺から張掖路を西へ進み、城隍廟と西関を経て橋へ向かう。旧城門は概略位置で、漢代金城県の治所も確定した城址として描かない。
caption.en: Walk west along Zhangye Road from the provincial-government area, pass the temple and Xiguan, then turn to the bridge. Former gates are approximate, and no certain Han Jincheng city is drawn.

p.src: Jincheng Commandery, established in 81 BCE, was a regional administration, not a single town inside today's Chengguan district. The seat of Jincheng County, its later movements, and the boundaries of modern Lanzhou are different questions. Some studies connect the early county seat with the Xigu area, while other identifications remain under debate; there is no responsible basis for drawing one certain Han city beneath Zhangye Road. The useful travel distinction is simple: treat the early geography towards Xigu separately from the later old-city core in front of you.

p.src: To connect the story with today's Chengguan old city, Wuquan matters more than the label Jincheng. Local gazetteers record Lanzhou under the Sui in 581 and the renaming of Jincheng County as Wuquan County in 583. In 619 the Tang made Wuquan the prefectural seat of Lanzhou, bringing the administrative focus into the area of present Chengguan. In 1081 the Song restored Lanzhou and its crossing facilities, then expanded a city site closer to the river. These points show administration and the crossing drawing together. At the river, read why the city opened towards the crossing; do not assume that any present street kept the same course from Sui or Tang times.

p.src: Local street-name records connect Qing-era Yuanmen Street and the old east-west main streets with sections of today's Zhangye Road. Walk west from the provincial-government area, use the City God Temple as the visible architectural layer midway, then turn from Xiguan towards the river. The former east and west gates on the map help estimate the width of the later walled core; no gate tower survives at those markers. If you reach the point and see no gate, you are not lost. Notice instead how the axis cuts through dense commerce, how courtyards withdraw behind the shopfront, and how close the old-city line comes to the river approach.

p.src: Lanzhou did not become a north-western administrative centre in one event in 1666. The Gansu governor moved here in 1666; the provincial civil administration followed from Gongchang in 1669; Lintao Prefecture moved and became Lanzhou Prefecture in 1738; and the Shaan-Gan governor-general was based here in 1764. There is no need to memorise all four dates. Keep the order: provincial, prefectural, and military institutions accumulated in stages, and more regional administration was handled in the city beside the crossing. The old office names, prefectural temple, and street axis around Zhangye Road belong to that accumulation, not to a single moment when a “capital was founded.”

p.src: Turn from Xiguan towards the Yellow River and the old-city axis soon meets the crossing. For centuries this point relied on a floating bridge and ferries. Completion of the permanent iron bridge in 1909 gave the central crossing a fixed steel structure instead of leaving it dependent only on waterborne facilities that required repeated maintenance. That did not make every ferry along the river disappear at once, but it provided a more stable route for people and goods through central Lanzhou. Stop at the south approach. This chapter explains why the bridge changed the city; Chapter 4 will inspect the trusses, deck, bank approaches, and practical route to White Pagoda Hill.

p.src: The iron bridge explains how the two banks connected; the railway explains why Lanzhou kept lengthening east and west. The Tian-Lan railway was completed at the end of 1952, bringing the Longhai line into Lanzhou. The 1954 plan then treated the old centre, the Xigu industrial district, the Qilihe rail and industrial district, and an eastern industrial district as distinct segments. A plan does not prove that every proposal was built exactly as drawn, but it shows that the scale of the city had moved beyond the old walls. That is why Lanzhou West, Gansu Provincial Museum, central Chengguan, and Lanzhou Railway Station in the east should still be planned as separate valley segments, not one short city-centre transfer.

p.src: At the south end of Zhongshan Bridge, keep only four layers: Han Jincheng is disputed regional geography; Wuquan and the later old city lie closer to the streets in front of you; Qing institutions concentrated in stages; and the bridge, railway, and planning stretched Lanzhou across the banks and along the valley. There is no need to add another dynasty or monument here. In Chapter 4, cross the bridge, compare the two bank approaches, and then choose how to climb White Pagoda Hill.
